facts.claim: "Drink a Beer" was written by Jim Beavers and Chris Stapleton.
Jim Beavers brought the finished chorus into the writing session. Stapleton says he took the verses in a morbid direction, about someone who had died.
Stapleton and Beavers were trying to write a song called "Drink A Beer" that wasn't a party song. They weighed celebrating a life event against remembering someone who had died.
Beavers said he and Stapleton skipped a full studio demo and made a simple guitar-and-vocal demo of the song.
Chris Stapleton sings background vocals on Bryan's recording. Bryan has said Stapleton is on the record and joined him at the CMA Awards.
The song was produced by Jeff Stevens and recorded in 2013 for Capitol Nashville.

The parent album Crash My Party was recorded at Ocean Way Nashville, Blackbird Studio and Starstruck Studios in Nashville. AllMusic lists Jody Stevens on programming and Tom Bukivac on guitar for the album.
It was released in November 2013 as the third single from Crash My Party and became Bryan's seventh number one on Billboard Country Airplay in February 2014.
Bryan has called the song "the coolest sad song ever". He connects with it because he lost both of his siblings.

Bryan's CMT performance of the song later became its music video, and it paid tribute to his late siblings Chris and Kelly. He only began speaking publicly about those losses in late 2013, around the time of the single.

research.lineage: A mainstream country ballad, a mournful song about drinking a beer in remembrance of someone who has died, which stands apart from the party-oriented songs that dominated Bryan's hits at the time.

draft:
The narrator of **Drink A Beer** gets bad news over the phone and does the most honest thing a grieving person can do: nothing useful. "So I just hung up the phone," Luke Bryan sings, and the song never pretends there was a better response available. There's no speech and no call to family. There's only a walk that ends at a pier, and a decision not to go home yet.

That restraint was the assignment. Chris Stapleton and Jim Beavers set out to write a song called "Drink A Beer" that wasn't a party song, and they weighed whether it should celebrate something or remember someone who'd died. Beavers walked in with the chorus already finished. Stapleton, by his own account, steered the verses somewhere morbid. The seam works in the song's favor. The chorus is a small ritual (sit, watch the sun go down, drink), and the verses supply the reason a person would need a ritual that small.

The second verse is where the feeling gets tangled. The narrator reaches for the standard comfort, that the good ones go too soon and the good Lord knows why, and then admits it isn't working. "I can't make it all make sense" lands like a correction of the line before it. Faith and refusal sit in the same breath, and neither wins. It's grief still trying to be polite and failing at it.

Jeff Stevens' production leaves plenty of air. Acoustic guitar strums, a bass walks underneath, and the drums hold a plain kick, snare and hi-hat pattern at a slow, easy pace. Bryan sings smooth and unhurried, with a little reverb around the voice, and never pushes. Stapleton is on the record too, singing background vocals, which fits a song he and Beavers first put down as a bare guitar-and-vocal demo.

Then the last chorus turns. After a plain goodbye, the narrator remembers "all the times that we used to," and the familiar chorus lines follow: sit on the pier, watch the sunset. The ritual invented to get through one afternoon turns out to be the one the two friends always shared. The walk wasn't an escape. It was a way back to the friend.

This came out as a single while party songs dominated Bryan's hits, and it still reached number one on Country Airplay. Bryan called it "the coolest sad song ever" and tied it to losing both of his siblings. His CMT performance, which became the video, honored Chris and Kelly at the time he first began speaking publicly about them. That history gives the song's plainness its weight.

The song gives you permission to grieve without finding the words, letting a beer and a sunset carry everything you can't say.
